title: Logs of the dead, and a shell in a shell-less pod
summary: logs --previous for crash loops, kubectl exec, and ephemeral debug containers for distroless images.

steps.title: What the container said, even after it died
body: kubectl logs deploy/api --previous        # -p: the last CRASHED container (the current one just restarted)
kubectl logs -l app=api --prefix --max-log-requests=10    # every pod with the label, lines tagged
kubectl exec -it deploy/api -- sh         # a shell, if the image has one
In a crash loop, plain `kubectl logs` shows the container that has just started and has probably printed only its
banner; `--previous` shows the one that died, with the error. The kubelet keeps one previous container per container.
Many production images (distroless, chiseled, static Go binaries) have **no shell**. `kubectl debug` adds an
**ephemeral container** with your tools to the running pod, without restarting it:
`--target` shares the target container's process namespace, so `ps` shows its processes and `/proc/1/root` is its
filesystem. Ephemeral containers cannot be removed; they disappear with the pod.

steps.prompt: A pod restarts every 30 seconds. `kubectl logs api-x` shows only `api 2.4 starting`. What next?
steps.explain: The current container has not crashed yet. `--previous` is the one that did, and its last lines say why. Deleting the pod throws away exactly that evidence.

steps.title: Read the crash and fix the config
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `api` is in `CrashLoopBackOff` after someone renamed a key in its
1. Write the error line the **crashed** container printed into `~/answers/fatal.txt`.
2. Fix the **ConfigMap** so the app finds the setting it asks for (keep the value it already has), and replace the pod
so it picks it up. The new pod must stay up.

checks.name: fatal.txt has the crashed container's error
checks.fail: Not the crash's error. `kubectl logs deploy/api --previous` shows what the last crashed container printed.

checks.name: api runs with DB_HOST from the ConfigMap
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=40s >/dev/null && sleep 3 && kubectl get pods -l app=api -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null)] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount' && kubectl logs $(kubectl get pods -l app=api -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null)] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .metadata.name') --tail=1
checks.fail: The new `api` pod should start without restarts and log `using database db.shop.svc.cluster.local`.

checks.name: the value comes from the ConfigMap
checks.fail: Put `DB_HOST` in the ConfigMap `api-config` (the app reads every key with `envFrom`).

hints: `kubectl get configmap api-config -o yaml`: the value is there under another key name.
`kubectl patch configmap api-config -p '{"data":{"DB_HOST":"db.shop.svc.cluster.local"}}'`, then `kubectl rollout restart deploy/api` (envFrom is read at start).
steps.explain: `--previous` turned "it keeps restarting" into one exact error line. The fix went into the ConfigMap, where the setting belongs, and `rollout restart` was needed because `envFrom` values are read when a container starts. Keeping the old key as well would also be fine during a migration; removing it is a separate, later change.

steps.title: Look inside a container that has no shell
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). The pod `edge` runs `traefik/whoami`, a single static binary: no shell,
no `ps`, no `cat`. Try `kubectl exec edge -- sh`: it fails. Nobody remembers which port it was started on.
1. Attach an **ephemeral debug container** from `busybox:1.37` to `edge`, targeting its container `edge`, without
2. From it, find the TCP port the app listens on, and write it into `~/answers/port.txt`.

checks.name: an ephemeral busybox container targets edge
checks.cmd: kubectl get pod edge -o json | jq -r '.spec.ephemeralContainers[]? | select(.targetContainerName == "edge") | .image' | sort -u
checks.fail: `edge` has no ephemeral container targeting `edge`. `kubectl debug edge --image=busybox:1.37 --target=edge ...`.

checks.name: the pod was not restarted
checks.fail: `edge` restarted. `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral container leaves the app running.

checks.name: port.txt is the listening port
checks.fail: Not the port. In the debug container: `netstat -tln`, or `cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '` to see the app's arguments.

hints: `kubectl debug -it edge --image=busybox:1.37 --target=edge -- sh` opens a shell next to the app.
This terminal is line based: `--attach=false -c dbg -- sleep 1h` starts it in the background, then `kubectl exec edge -c dbg -- netstat -tln`.
With `--target`, the app is PID 1 in the debug container's view: `cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '`.
solution: kubectl exec edge -c dbg -- sh -c "cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\\0' ' '"
steps.explain: Ephemeral containers are how you debug minimal images in production: you bring the tools, the image stays small, and the pod keeps running. `--target` shares the process namespace, so you see the app's processes, its arguments, and its filesystem under `/proc/1/root`. For a broken node, `kubectl debug node/NAME -it --image=busybox:1.37` does the same on the host.
